Karthik Narasimhan: Yeah. I think the this is something I tweeted back when, when we released Tau Bench as well. One of the interesting, or I would say, like, the most exciting things to take from the whole, like, Tau Bench paper is the fact that we can just simulate users really well now, right? And I know it seems like a small thing, and user simulation is not a new thing. People have worked on it for decades. But the fact that you can do it with such high fidelity has great implications. Because if you think about how AI systems are gonna be used in the future, they're not gonna be in isolation. There's always gonna be a human interacting with the systems at some level, right? This was always something we put off before because the model was just not good enough.

Right? You're like, "Oh, why are you talking about human-AI interaction when the AI can't even do two things," right? But I think we're in this phase now where that's gonna be critical, and that just means that all your evals are not just going to be like "Hey, I collected a data set, and it's a static data set, and I just run the model through it." We have to have more dynamic evals. And I think that's where these kind of like simulations are where, where you're basically having dynamic interactions between different models. It can be as simple as a user simulator or it could be more competitive, like multi-agent cooperative or competitive multi-agent systems and all that. So there's this whole, like, spectrum where you can slide the slider. But I think that's definitely the way that we're gonna go in the future, right?

And in the future we'll also have humans ideally interacting with the systems live, right? And having that be part of the eval. But that requires a different skill.

So I think it was pretty exciting even back then because it was kind of clear that using a transformer, you can go way further than LSTM which were the state of the art back then, right? That was kind of the motivation towards what can you do to train these models safely using RL, POLCO, and all of that.

And then I think yeah, and then it was like as these models evolved, right, like the whole scaling paradigm had started. 2019, '20, '21. We were seeing two, three, even the BERT based models were expanding in size and all of that. So I think they were becoming increasingly capable. And it was reaching the point where and it was clear, more and more clear that some of the things that I had wanted to do even back in the PhD. So in text UK, IQN, you can actually think of as like a very rudimentary demonstration of an LLM based agent, right? So it's like it's used the language model to predict things, read text on the text games in RL. But it's, like, very, very rudimentary. It didn't work at all. Like it's like I mean, if you, if you look at that right now, you'll just laugh, right?

It's like, okay, what? But as these models get gone really powerful, right, you have this, like, LLM which has a lot of the right priors. A lot of things change, right? So RL, you don't assume any priors. But with an LLM, you have a lot of the right priors, a lot of the right heuristics. So you can actually do many of these things that we've always dreamt of doing, right? And so it was apparent to me, like, hey, we need to be able to, like, first off, put out the right benchmarks that need to, that need to really push these boundaries, right? So WebShop, for example, was one where, like, yeah, there's a really nice paper by folks at OpenAI. The mini world of this. But it was too rudimentary, too small again, right? So we were like, okay, take this, make it into a realistic task, like shop on Amazon.

Can these models do it, right? And they actually turned out they were not bad, right? So. So I'd say, like, most of the recent stuff for me has been not just to perform research in an isolation, but I think I would actually look at, like, what is something that can have impact. Doesn't have to have immediate impact, but even a few years down the line, right? Something that's more realistic. Let's push the boundaries here, and I think these models are incredibly smart, incredibly capable. None: Mm-hmm. Awesome. And I guess like, I mean, these days, you know, we have, you know, SWE-bench. Like there's one argument that is like, okay, can your benchmark, like in a statistically significant way, separate out two different models and their capabilities? So if like every model is getting 100%, then obviously that's not a great benchmark. But like also, you know, say your benchmark is, you know, we want to evaluate tool use or tool calls, for instance. Um, or say for instance, you know, there is some qualitative characteristic that you want your benchmark to measure. Um, just because your benchmark statistically significantly, um, you know, separates two different models doesn't necessarily mean that it's separating them in the right way, AKA, that the benchmark is actually serving its intended qualitative purpose. And so there's like no real way to know what the answer is of how to build the right benchmark, 'cause there's no real way to know whether the benchmark you've constructed is the right benchmark. It's a different thing to say like, okay, you know, so model A and model B are both competing on the same benchmark. Model A does better than model B. But now the question is how do you construct a benchmark that is actually, you know, like it serves the purpose that it's intended to serve of what it's trying to model. I'm sure there's infinite other benchmarks that your lab is about to come up with. So how do you think about it?

Karthik Narasimhan: So I think a benchmark can serve multiple purposes. And it's important to distinguish those purposes, I think. Right? So on the one hand, there is the quantitative aspect of it where like you sort of have a leaderboard and you could be like, "Oh, this model is number three, and this model is number two, and there's the gap of two points between them." I think that's useful as a ranking mechanism. There's a different purpose, right? The other purpose is also just to showcase a sort of task or a capability which is useful, and like you want the, you want the model to get better at that, right? Any model. It doesn't matter which model. You just want to climb to 100%, right? So I feel like people also look at benchmarks in one of these two angles, right?

To me, the more interesting angle is the second one, which is you feel like there's some capability that the model could have, but it's probably maybe currently lacking. Maybe it's not like all the way there, but you want to push the community towards like improving on that, right? And so I try to go for those, those kind of tasks where like it seems like- Hey, why are we not working on this thing? So a benchmark is a good way to sort of kickstart more community involvement there. I think ranking part is useful, right? Obviously, it's useful when you sort of benchmark your model against your competitor's model or somebody else's model. But beyond a certain point I don't think you wanna you know, wanna over-rotate on those results, right? Like, if you're at 20% and then you go up to, like, 80%, that's great.

You-- your model, that's a very clear signal. But if everyone's at 80% and you're climbing to 81 and 82 I mean, at that point there are all benchmarks get saturated, all benchmarks have issues. So at that point, it's probably worth your time to actually look at the next thing, right? So I think those are some principles in hindsight that I feel like they're worth, like thinking about.

Like, make it make us move from being like, "Okay, generate one function piece of code and then test it," to actually solving more realistic SWE, SWE tasks, right? astra.text:
Yeah, I think there are a couple of things there, right? One is that coding has this really nice property where you can execute something and get feedback. But even there, passing the tests doesn't necessarily mean you've done everything the user wanted, right? So it's a very useful signal, but it's still a proxy for the actual thing you care about.

And I think for other domains, you want to ask a similar question: what can you actually observe about whether the task was completed? Customer support is one example, which is what we were looking at with Tau Bench. You can have a conversation that sounds really nice, but did you actually make the change the customer requested? Did you follow the policies? Those are things you can check by looking at what happened in the environment, beyond just reading the conversation.

Accounting could have some of those properties as well, right? If you're reconciling transactions, there are concrete things you can verify. But then maybe there's missing information, and you need to ask somebody for a document or clarify what a particular expense was. Now you're evaluating not just whether the model can do the calculation, but whether it can get the information it needs to do the calculation correctly. And that's where this interaction aspect becomes really interesting to me.

So I wouldn't necessarily start with, like, ‘Let's evaluate an entire accountant,’ right? I'd start with useful tasks that are part of that work, build an environment where you can actually perform those tasks, and then expand from there. That's sort of the philosophy behind the benchmarks we've been talking about.

The difficult part is making that environment realistic. What information does the agent have access to? What can it change? Are there multiple valid ways to finish? And then there are aspects where you probably do need human judgment. You can't necessarily reduce everything to one automatic check.

But I don't think that means we should wait until we can evaluate the whole job perfectly. You can make progress on pieces of it. For me, the exciting direction is tasks where the agent has to work with somebody over time, clarify what they want, take actions, and respond when something changes. Because that's much closer to how these systems are actually going to be useful.

sol.text:
Yeah, I think coding is kind of the ideal first domain because, like you said, the environment is digital, the actions are all observable, and you often have an executable verifier. You can run the tests and get a reasonably objective signal. But even there, right, passing the tests is not the same as producing maintainable, secure, efficient code. So the moment you move beyond coding, that gap between what is easy to measure and what we actually care about becomes even larger.

I think the next set of tasks will be things like customer support, accounting, finance operations, maybe legal or research workflows—areas where most of the work already happens through digital systems and there are policies, records, and relatively clear outcomes. But the benchmark cannot just ask the model one question and compare its answer to a reference. You need to put the agent in an environment, give it tools and incomplete information, simulate the other people involved, and evaluate the whole trajectory. Did it gather the right information? Did it follow policy? Did it make the correct updates? Did it ask for clarification when necessary? Did it avoid taking an irreversible action without approval? And maybe did it complete the task with a reasonable amount of time and cost?

That is part of what is interesting about the conversational and dual-control setting. In many real jobs, the agent does not control the entire environment. The user has private information and may need to take actions too. So success depends on communication and coordination, not simply on whether the model knows the answer. Accounting is a good example: the final number might be easy to check, but the hard part is collecting the right documents, resolving inconsistencies, following the appropriate procedure, and escalating an ambiguous case.

Then as you move toward something like construction, robotics, or healthcare, you need richer simulation, multimodal observations, longer time horizons, and probably humans in the evaluation loop. The feedback is also delayed, and failures can be costly, so you cannot learn by breaking the building a thousand times. I don't think that makes evaluation impossible; it just means there probably isn't one scalar metric or one static benchmark. You need a collection of tests for outcomes, process, safety, robustness, and human judgment.

So, yeah, I think the middle is basically these digitally mediated workflows where we can build reasonably faithful environments today. And the broader research problem is: how do we turn more of the messy real world into an evaluation environment without simplifying away the exact capabilities we wanted to measure?

opus.text:
Yeah, I think that's a great framing, and I'd actually push back slightly on the "technical" axis. I don't think it's technicality, right? I think the axis is really verifiability. Like, coding got there first not because it's the hardest or the most technical thing, but because you have a compiler and you have unit tests, right? Somebody else already built the verifier for you. It's free. And the whole task lives inside a computer, so the environment is basically free too. So you get both halves of the benchmark for nothing, and that's, that's a very unusual gift.

So then the question becomes, okay, what are the other jobs where the work leaves some kind of auditable trace, right? And there are actually a lot of them. Like, this was one of the tricks in Tau-bench, if you think about it. We didn't try to grade the conversation. Grading a conversation is horrible, right? Like, was the agent polite, was it helpful, whatever, you're immediately in LLM-as-a-judge land and it's mushy. What we did instead was we just checked the state of the database at the end. Did the flight actually get cancelled? Was the refund actually issued? And that generalizes surprisingly far, because so much white collar work is basically mutating some system of record, right? A CRM, a ledger, an EHR, a ticketing system, a spreadsheet. If you can snapshot the world before and after, you don't need to judge the process, you just check the outcome.

So accounting is actually a great example, and I think it's much closer to coding than people assume. Reconciliation has a ground truth, right? The books either balance or they don't. Same with a lot of financial analysis, a lot of ops work, a lot of the back office stuff in healthcare, like prior auth and coding and billing. Legal is interesting because contract review has this nice property that lawyers already produce redlines, so there's a, there's a human artifact you can compare against, even if it's not unique. And then it gets progressively worse as you go. Scientific research, like, reproducing a paper's results, that's checkable. Coming up with a good research idea, that's, that's not checkable, at least not in any timeframe you'd want for a benchmark.

But honestly, I think the bottleneck for all of these is not the metric. It's the environment. That's the thing people underestimate. For SWE-bench you had GitHub, right? Millions of repos with issues and the corresponding PRs and tests sitting right there. There is no GitHub for accounting. So somebody has to go build a realistic sandbox with a fake company that has a plausible chart of accounts and messy vendor invoices and, and all of that, and you need actual domain experts in the room, and that is expensive and it's slow and it's not the kind of thing that gets you a paper in six weeks. Which is exactly why I think academia has under-invested here and why a lot of the good stuff is gonna come out of, of places that have the domain access.

And then the other thing which I think is genuinely unsolved, and this goes back to what we were talking about with dual control, is that in a real job the spec is underspecified. Like, nobody hands an accountant a well-formed issue with a failing test. You get a Slack message that says "hey, can you look at Q3, something's off," and half the job is figuring out what the question even is, and knowing who to go ask. That's the part I don't think we have any good benchmark for yet. And I suspect the way you get there is exactly through these simulated multi-party setups, where the information the agent needs is not in the prompt, it's distributed across other agents that you have to go interrogate. That, to me, is the interesting frontier, much more than adding another coding benchmark.

grok.text:
Yeah, I think that’s a really good way of putting it. Coding is special, right? You have this extremely nice property that the artifact is executable. You can run tests, you can look at diffs, you can say pass or fail in a pretty crisp way. And because it’s all text, the whole loop sits inside a computer already. So I think that’s why SWE-style tasks were the first ones that really took off as agent benchmarks. It’s not that coding is the only important job. It’s that it’s the job where evaluation is least ambiguous.

But I wouldn’t say the rest of knowledge work is hopeless, and I also wouldn’t say you have to jump all the way to a construction site. There’s a pretty large middle, and a lot of what we’ve been doing is exactly in that middle. WebShop was shopping. Tau Bench, Tau Squared, the Sierra work — that’s customer support. That’s not writing a function and running pytest. It’s a person, a policy, a set of tools, a database, a messy conversation. And at the end you can still check something concrete. Did the refund go through for the right amount? Did they follow the policy? Is the backend in the right state? The dialogue can be fuzzy, but the outcome doesn’t have to be.

So the trick, at least the way I think about it, is: find domains where the *process* is linguistic and interactive, but the *world* still has structure you can inspect. Accounting is actually a pretty good example of that. Numbers have to add up. There’s a ledger. There are constraints, tax rules, double-entry, all of that. You can imagine an agent talking to a user, pulling records, posting entries, and you evaluate whether the books are consistent and whether the right actions were taken. Legal is a bit further out, because there’s more genuine judgment and the ground truth is mushier. Something like a recruiter or a project manager is in between — lots of communication, lots of tools, some artifacts you can check, but also taste and context. And then as you go toward physical work, now you need simulators, perception, robotics, safety, the whole stack. That’s a different problem. I wouldn’t start there if the goal is a good agent benchmark tomorrow.

The problems that show up, I think, are pretty consistent across that middle band. One, you don’t get a unit test for free, so you have to decide what success even means — database state, policy compliance, user goal, some mix. Two, a lot of the information lives with the human, and they don’t hand you a spec. They ramble, they omit things, they change their mind. That’s why I care so much about user simulation and this dual-control setup, because a static dataset just doesn’t capture that. Three, these tasks are long-horizon and stateful. You can do the right thing on turn three and blow it on turn twelve. Four, the constraints are written in natural language, not in a test suite, so the agent has to actually *read* and follow a policy, which is a very different skill from generating a patch.

Are we working on it? Yeah. Tau Bench came out of exactly this gap at Sierra — we needed evals for production agents that were not coding agents. Tau Squared is pushing on the interactive, dual-control side of that. I think other people are doing adjacent things: computer use, browsing, office workflows, all of that. I don’t think we have the accounting benchmark yet in the way we have SWE-bench, and I think that’s a real opening, because it has more verifiability than people assume. But I also wouldn’t overfit to “one benchmark per job title.” The more useful question is, what’s a realistic workflow with tools, memory, a human in the loop, and a checkable end state — and then build that. Coding was the first one because it was the easiest to check. Customer support, ops, finance, these tool-using white-collar workflows — that’s the middle. And I think that’s where a lot of the next evals should live.

gemini.text:
Yeah, I think you hit the nail on the head, right? Code is really unique because it comes with a built-in verifier: the compiler and the test suite. It's binary. You run `pytest`, and either the tests pass or they don't, which gives you this nice, objective ground truth that makes benchmark creation much cleaner.

When you move into the middle ground—things like accounting, finance, operations, customer support, or general knowledge work—it gets much trickier. And I think there are two or three major challenges that we have to solve there.

The first one is the verification problem. In code, you have unit tests. But in accounting or data analysis, what is the unit test? Often, there are multiple valid paths to arrive at an answer, or the output is a complex artifact like a financial model, a slide deck, or an updated database. If you don't have deterministic assertions, you end up having to rely on things like LLM-as-a-judge, which has its own biases, or manual human evaluation, which doesn't scale. So finding ways to verify state changes programmatically—did the agent correctly modify the database or balance the ledger according to the constraints?—is a big open problem.

The second challenge is the environment and tool grounding. Most of this knowledge work doesn't happen in a vacuum or in a clean Python script. People are using spreadsheets, ERP systems, Salesforce, Slack, email, web portals. Setting up realistic, reproducible sandboxes that simulate that software stack—with state, persistence, and safe API hooks—is a massive engineering effort. That was actually a big motivation behind things like WebShop and Tau-Bench: how do we create an environment that simulates the tools and database state of real-world workflows without having to hook it directly into a live production system?

And then the third piece is the interaction side, which we touched upon earlier. Real-world tasks aren't static. In accounting or legal work, the initial prompt you get is almost never complete. A client or manager gives you vague requirements, and a good human agent asks clarifying questions, deals with missing documents, and adapts to feedback. 

So yeah, I think people are definitely working on this—whether it's computer-use benchmarks, browser navigation, or enterprise agent evals. But until we crack automatic verification and build really good, stateful simulation environments for these workflows, it's going to be much harder to make progress there than it has been in coding.

kimi.text:
Yeah, no, that's a great question, and I think you've hit on, like, the crux of it, right? Which is verifiability. Like, the reason coding took off first is that you have this really crisp signal. You run the tests, they pass or they fail, right? And everything lives in text. So I think of it as, like, a spectrum. On one end you have tasks that are fully digital and fully verifiable, like code and math. And on the other end you have, like, the construction worker example, where the task is physical, the feedback is messy, and honestly we have no idea how to even build the simulator for that yet, right?

So the middle is, I think, where things get really interesting, and the middle is basically, like, digital knowledge work. So accounting, ops, procurement, travel, customer support, which is obviously what we were doing at Sierra. And the reason those are tractable is that even though the job feels fuzzy, the work actually happens inside software. Like, an accountant isn't doing accounting in the physical world, they're doing it inside some system with ledgers and databases, right? And so you can actually build benchmarks where the verification isn't pass-fail unit tests, but it's checking the final state of the world. Like, did the refund actually get issued? Do the books actually balance? Was the right policy followed? That was kind of the insight behind Tau Bench, right? You define the environment, you define the rules, and then you check whether the end state is correct.

Now, the problems with building those benchmarks are pretty real. One is just that building the environment is expensive. Code has this amazing property that GitHub is just, like, sitting there with millions of realistic tasks. But if you want to do accounting, somebody has to go build a realistic sandbox of an entire enterprise system with realistic data, and that's a huge amount of engineering work. Second, access. The actual workflows of these jobs are proprietary. Companies don't want to open-source how they handle exceptions or what their policies are, right? So academics often don't even know what the real task distribution looks like. And honestly, that's why I think these kinds of benchmarks are gonna come from, like, partnerships between industry and academia, kind of similar to how Tau Bench came out of actually deploying agents at Sierra.

And then the third thing is that a lot of these jobs are fundamentally interactive. Like, the hard part of the job is not balancing the ledger, it's, like, dealing with the ambiguous email from the client, or figuring out which exception applies. And so the eval has to be dynamic, right? Which goes back to what we were talking about with user simulation. Like, you can't just have a static dataset, you need the agent to actually talk to people, ask clarifying questions, handle pushback. And then, yeah, there's this whole other question of circularity, where now you're using models to evaluate models, and you have to be really careful about that, right?

So, yeah, I think accounting is a great example of what's next, and broadly I'd say the community and we are both thinking about moving from these, like, single-agent static tasks to, like, full workflow-level things where the agent is orchestrating across tools and people over long horizons. But the ordering you're describing is exactly right, like, the degree to which a job lives in software is basically the degree to which we can benchmark it today. Right?

fable.text:
Yeah, so I think that's a great question, and I think the framing you have is roughly right, but I would refine it a little bit. Like, I don't think it's really about how technical the job is. I think it's about how verifiable the outcome is, right? So coding just happens to be this, like, sweet spot where the input is text, the output is text, and you have this oracle, right? You have unit tests. You run the code, and it either passes or it doesn't. And the interesting thing is even that is not fully clean, right? Like, if you look at SWE-bench, we spent a lot of time on, like, are the tests actually testing the right thing? Is the issue underspecified? Is there more than one valid patch? So even in the best case, like, the evaluation is a lot messier than people think.

But yeah, so then the question is what's in the middle, right? And I think there's a whole spectrum. So if you think about something like accounting or, like, tax preparation or even, like, legal work, a lot of that is actually more verifiable than people assume, right? Like, there is a right answer. There are rules. There's a ground truth state that you can check. And I would actually put Tau Bench in that category, right? Like, customer service is not a technical job, but we found a way to evaluate it. And the way we did it is basically you look at the state of the world, right? So you're not grading the conversation. You're not saying, like, "Oh, was the agent polite?" You're saying, at the end of this interaction, is the database in the state it should be in? Did the flight get changed? Did the refund get issued to the right account? Did it follow the policy or did it just give in to the user? And that turns out to be a really clean signal, right? So I think that, that trick of, like, converting a fuzzy job into "what is the state of the world after you're done" actually generalizes to a lot of things. Like, you can think of, like, ops jobs, back-office jobs, anything that touches a system of record. I think a lot of enterprise work looks like that, honestly. And people don't realize this, but, like, a huge fraction of white-collar work is basically someone reading some text, making a decision, and then updating some system, right? So that's, like, very much in reach.

Then you have the harder part of the middle, which is the stuff where there's no single right answer, right? So like writing a research report or, like, doing analysis or, like, giving advice. And there I think you basically have two options, and both of them are imperfect. One is you use rubrics, right? So like a human expert writes down, "Here are the ten things a good answer should have," and then you have a model grade against that. And that works okay, but the problem is, like, the rubric is never complete, and the models figure out how to game the rubric. And the other is you go to, like, pairwise preference or, like, human judgments, which is what a lot of the chatbot arena style things do, and that has its own issues with, like, you're measuring what people like rather than what's actually correct.

And then I would say there's actually a third axis that I think is more interesting than the verification part, which is the time horizon and the interaction. Right? Like, the reason coding was tractable is not just that you can run the code. It's that the task is, like, one shot. Here's an issue, go fix it, come back. But most real jobs are not like that, right? Like, an accountant's job is not "close the books." It's, like, three months of, like, back and forth with people and, like, waiting for documents and asking clarifying questions and dealing with someone giving you the wrong thing. So the eval has to be dynamic. And this is actually why I keep going back to the user simulation thing, right? Because if you can simulate the other people in the loop with high fidelity, then suddenly you can evaluate these long-horizon, messy, interactive jobs, and you're not just, like, giving the model a document and asking it to produce a document.

And yeah, we are working on stuff in this direction, both at Princeton and I think a lot of other folks are too. Like, I'll say the thing that we're struggling with is not really the model side. It's the construction side, right? Like, to build one of these things well you need actual domain experts. You need someone who's done accounting for twenty years to tell you, like, what the edge cases are, what actually matters, what a junior person gets wrong. And that's expensive and slow, and the academic community is not really set up for it, right? Like, it's easy for us to build a coding benchmark because we're all coders. It's much harder to build a benchmark for, like, insurance claims adjustment. So I actually think the bottleneck for the next set of benchmarks is less about the AI and more about, like, going and finding the people who actually know these jobs and getting them in the room.

And then the last thing I'd say is, like, the construction worker example you gave. I actually don't think it's that far off in a sense. Like, for physical stuff you obviously have the embodiment problem and all that. But the evaluation question is the same, right? Like, is the building standing? Did it pass inspection? Those are verifiable states of the world. The hard part is the interaction with the environment, not the grading. So I think, like, if you squint, the pattern is the same everywhere. Find the state that matters, figure out how to check it, and then simulate everything around it well enough that the model has to actually do the job rather than just, like, produce something that looks like the job.
